questions.stem: A 44-year-old woman presented with a 4-day history of fevers, malaise, and redness around the site of a longterm indwelling IV line in place for cancer chemotherapy. She had a history of metastatic cervical cancer. She had no known drug allergies. On physical exam, some purulence was expressed from the IV line site. Investigations: Total white cell count 12.5 ×109/L Hemoglobin 8.5 g/dL Platelets 55 ×109/L Creatinine 0.8 mg/dL Gram-stain of exit site pus showed GPC in clusters Blood cultures obtained through both the longterm indwelling IV line, as well from a peripheral vein, were positive for Staphylococcus aureus, with susceptibilities pending
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial empiric treatment of this patient’s bacteremia?
questions.explanation: Vancomycin Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) must be covered empirically, pending sensitivities. Dalbavancin is not established for treatment of infections other than acute bacterial skin/skin structure infections. Linezolid should be avoided for treatment of line-related bacteremias due to inferior efficacy in that setting. Clindamycin is not as reliably active against MRSA as vancomycin and is not established as a preferred treatment for MRSA bloodstream infection. There are no apparent contraindications or concerns with using vancomycin in this case.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 1 Q4

questions.stem: An 11-month-old boy developed a high fever. This was associated with malaise, irritability, and poor feeding. After 48 hours he developed a macular rash along his arms and legs. There was extensive confluent blistering of the perineum, but otherwise the trunk and back were spared. There were no lesions on his scalp. There were a number of perioral lesions but no lesions visible inside the mouth. Some of the lesions progressed into thin-walled vesicles containing clear fluid. There were macules on the soles of his feet. The fever resolved 24 hours after the rash appeared. The rash took 10 days to clear but left no scars. Three weeks later the skin on his feet began to desquamate. He attended a nursery for 3 days a week. He had had his vaccinations as per the UK schedule for his age. He had been born at full term and was meeting his developmental milestones. He lived at home with two older siblings.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely pathogen?
questions.explanation: Coxsackievirus A6 This is a case of hand, foot, and mouth disease (HMFD), most commonly caused by Coxsackieviruses A10, A6, A16, and enterovirus A71. Outbreaks are commonly associated with daycare centers among others, and in infants and children under the age of 5.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 7 Q44

questions.stem: A 71-year-old woman presented with fevers and a discharging wound on her right calf. She had a recent right calf fasciotomy due to a popliteal thrombus and end-stage renal disease on regular thrice-weekly conventional hemodialysis. She had no known drug allergies. On examination her temperature was 38.6°C, and there was purulent discharge from her right calf incision site. Investigations: Total white blood cell count 12,500 cells/mm3 Wound swab culture: positive for methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA) 2/2 blood cultures positive for MSSA
questions.lead_in: What would be most appropriate for thrice-weekly posthemodialysis dosing for treatment of this patient’s infection, assuming a planned duration of therapy of 4–6 weeks?
questions.explanation: Cefazolin Ceftazidime is only marginally active against MSSA and would not be appropriate. Linezolid dosing is unaffected by renal insufficiency or dialysis and should not be given just postdialysis. Oritavancin is not established for treatment of MSSA bacteremia nor for treatment courses of 4–6 weeks in length. Vancomycin has been found to be clinically inferior to beta-lactams (including cefazolin) for MSSA infection in patients with end-stage renal diseases on regular thriceweekly hemodialysis. Cefazolin postdialysis dosing has been shown to be effective for MSSA bacteremia in patients with end-stage renal disease.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 8 Q2

questions.stem: A 22-year-old man presented with a painful swelling on his thigh. He denied any associated fevers or chills. The patient had applied warm compresses to the site for the past two days with little improvement. He was normally well and did not take any regular medication. On examination, there was a 3-cm lesion on his right inner thigh. The lesion was warm, tender, and fluctuant to palpation. The rest of his physical examination was unremarkable.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: Hold antibiotics pending results of a superficial swab MCS
Incision and drainage at the bedside
List for urgent surgical debridement in an operating room

questions.explanation: Incision and drainage at the bedside A carbuncle of this size is likely to respond well to bedside incision and drainage. Antibiotics alone are unlikely to address the infection, and surgical debridement of the carbuncle and/or hospitalization to receive intravenous antibiotics for a lesion of this size is not indicated, particularly given that the patient does not have any systemic signs of infection (e.g., fevers, chills). Superficial skin cultures are likely to grow commensal flora; abscess cultures are preferred to guide antibiotic therapy.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 2 Q23

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man was admitted with a 1-week history of nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, dry cough, fever, chills, and myalgia. He was beginning to feel better until 48 hours ago when he developed recurrence of fever and chills, a productive cough with blood-streaked sputum, and right-sided pleuritic chest pain. On physical examination, his temperature was 38.8°C, blood pressure 100/50 mmHg, pulse rate 110/minute, and respiration rate 24/minute. CXR: right middle lobe airspace disease with a small area of cavitation as well as blunting of the right costophrenic angle.
questions.lead_in: What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.explanation: Vancomycin, ceftriaxone, and azithromycin This patient has a classic presentation for a postinfluenza or viral illness with initial flu-like symptoms progressing to worsening fever, productive cough, and imaging findings suggestive of a pleural effusion. Although the infection could be due to Streptococcus pneumoniae, there is concern for postinfluenza Staphylococcus aureus pneumonia, and the patient requires empiric coverage for MRSA. Although daptomycin does provide MRSA coverage, it is inactivated in the lung by surfactant and would be a poor choice in this clinical scenario.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 8 Q5

questions.question: There is an MRSA cluster in the neonatal nursery.

parts.text: What are 2 outbreak patterns that could be suggestive of a common source infection?
2 phenotypic and 2 genotypic methods to type MRSA.

questions.model_answer:
a) Outbreak patterns suggestive of a common source: (1) A point-source epidemic curve - a sharp, single peak of cases clustered within one incubation period. (2) All cases sharing a single identifiable common exposure (e.g., the same piece of equipment, healthcare worker, or product) rather than a stepwise/propagated pattern of secondary transmission.
b) Phenotypic typing methods: antibiogram (antimicrobial susceptibility pattern) and phage typing. Genotypic typing methods: pulsed-field gel electrophoresis (PFGE) and spa typing (or multilocus sequence typing/whole-genome sequencing).

parts.text: 17. In patients who have S. aureus bacteremia, list five reasons to do a TEE if the TTE is negative. (5)

questions.model_answer: Indications to pursue TEE despite a negative TTE in S. aureus bacteremia: (1) Presence of a prosthetic valve or intracardiac device (pacemaker/ICD leads) - TTE has poor sensitivity for these. (2) Poor TTE image quality/inadequate windows (e.g., obesity, COPD, mechanical ventilation). (3) High clinical suspicion for IE (e.g., persistent bacteremia beyond 72 hours despite appropriate therapy, or new murmur). (4) Evidence of metastatic/embolic complications (septic emboli, vertebral osteomyelitis, splenic infarcts). (5) Hemodialysis-dependent patients or other high-risk features (community acquisition without an identifiable removable focus), since TTE alone is inadequate to exclude IE and change the planned duration of therapy in these higher-risk situations.

questions.question: Staph aureus.

parts.text: Explain mechanism of VISA and VRSA.
Give MIC cut offs.

questions.model_answer:
a) Mechanism: VISA (vancomycin-intermediate S. aureus, also called GISA) arises from pleiotropic chromosomal mutations (e.g., vraSR, graSR, walKR) that cause a thickened cell wall with an increased number of free, non-cross-linked D-ala-D-ala termini. These act as decoy/false targets that trap vancomycin molecules in the outer cell wall layers, preventing the drug from reaching its site of action at the cytoplasmic membrane. VRSA arises from acquisition of the vanA gene cluster (via transfer from vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus), which produces altered peptidoglycan precursors ending in D-ala-D-lactate instead of D-ala-D-alanine, dramatically reducing vancomycin binding affinity.
b) MIC cutoffs: susceptible ≤2 µg/mL; VISA (intermediate) 4-8 µg/mL; VRSA (resistant) ≥16 µg/mL. hVISA (heteroresistant) = bulk MIC ≤2 µg/mL but harbours a resistant subpopulation detectable by population analysis profile.

questions.question: MRSA is bad.

parts.text: Name 3 reasons to prevent nosocomial MRSA infection
List 6 integral components of IPC to prevent nosocomial transmission of MRSA in acute care

questions.model_answer:
a) Reasons to prevent nosocomial MRSA infection: (1) MRSA infection is associated with increased morbidity and mortality compared to susceptible S. aureus. (2) It increases length of hospital stay and healthcare costs. (3) Colonized/infected patients act as a reservoir for ongoing transmission to other vulnerable patients within the facility.
b) Six integral IPC components to prevent nosocomial MRSA transmission in acute care: (1) Hand hygiene. (2) Contact precautions for colonized/infected patients. (3) Active surveillance screening/testing of high-risk patients on admission. (4) Single room accommodation or cohorting of positive patients. (5) Thorough environmental cleaning and disinfection of the patient environment/equipment. (6) Antimicrobial stewardship (and/or decolonization protocols and staff education).

questions.question: 6 yo with diffuse rash, low grade fevers and bullae. Cultures from the bullae grow Staphylococcus aureus.

parts.text: What is clinical syndrome?
Name 2 Virulence factors (2)
Describe the mechanisms of action of the virulence factors
Name 1 sign associated with the disease and describe it.

questions.model_answer:
a) Clinical syndrome: bullous impetigo (localized staphylococcal skin infection with toxin-mediated intraepidermal bullae; S. aureus is recoverable directly from the bullae, distinguishing it from generalized staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome where distant skin is affected by circulating toxin and cultures of the skin/bullae are typically sterile).
b) 2 virulence factors: exfoliative toxin A (ETA) and exfoliative toxin B (ETB).
c) Mechanism of action: ETA and ETB are serine proteases that specifically cleave desmoglein-1, a desmosomal cadherin responsible for keratinocyte adhesion in the superficial epidermis (stratum granulosum), causing intraepidermal splitting and blister/bulla formation.
d) Associated sign: Nikolsky sign - gentle lateral/tangential pressure on apparently normal perilesional skin causes the superficial epidermis to shear and slough off, reflecting the loss of keratinocyte adhesion.

questions.question: 6 years old comes in with bullae and desquamating rash that started in face and then spread to trunks and extremities. Raw skin after bullae erupts. Bullae and desquamation mainly at the flexor surfaces. Culture of fluid from ruptured bullae grows S aureus, which is unusual, as the bullae are supposed to be sterile.

parts.text: What is the syndrome
What are the two key toxins responsible for this
Describe mechanism of how the toxins led to the presentation
What is the sign on clinical exam, name it and describe it

cohort_answer.text: Syndrome: Staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome. Toxins: Exfoliative toxin A and B (ETA and ETB) (for food borne infection its Staph enterotoxins; for toxic shock its TSST-1 toxic shock syndrome toxin-1, a superantigen). Mechanism: Toxins released by Staph locally pass through body to act on stratum granulosum of the epidermis (hence cultures being negative), targeting desmoglein-1 (Dsg-1) which is important in maintaining intrakeratinocyte adhesion. Toxin is a protease that cleaves this, hence the desquamation. Sign: Nikolsky sign - top layers of skin slides away from lower layers when rubbed

questions.question: Regarding Vancomycin Intermediate Staph aureus

parts.text: How would you define heterogeneous vancomycin-intermediate Staphylococcus aureus?
What is the MIC for VISA?
describe the mechanism of resistance of VISA as it applies to 1) the cell wall 2) Vancomycin?

questions.model_answer:
a) hVISA definition: a S. aureus isolate whose bulk population vancomycin MIC tests susceptible (≤2 µg/mL) by standard methods, but which contains a subpopulation of cells (typically at a frequency of about 10^-6) capable of growing at vancomycin concentrations in the intermediate/VISA range, detectable only by population analysis profiling (not by routine susceptibility testing).
b) MIC for VISA: 4-8 µg/mL.
c) Mechanism of resistance: (1) Cell wall - VISA develops a markedly thickened cell wall containing an increased number of free, non-cross-linked D-ala-D-ala peptidoglycan termini, resulting from chromosomal mutations in regulatory systems (vraSR, graSR, walKR) that alter cell wall synthesis/turnover; (2) Vancomycin - the abundant free D-ala-D-ala residues in the thickened outer wall act as decoy/false binding targets, trapping and sequestering vancomycin molecules before they can penetrate to reach the actively growing cell wall synthesis sites at the cytoplasmic membrane, effectively reducing the amount of free drug able to reach its target (affinity trapping/clogging mechanism), rather than true alteration of the drug's ultimate target.

questions.question: Superantigens - S. aureus

parts.text: Aside from TSST-1 and toxic shock syndrome, name one other S. aureus superantigen and its associated syndrome?
What is the mechanism of action of superantigens?

cohort_answer.text: A) SEA, SEB, SEC, SED - food poisoning, TSS; Exfoliative Toxin A and B - Scalded Skin Syndrome; TSST-1 - TSS. B) Non-specific excessive activation of T-cells causing polyclonal T cell activation and massive cytokine release; superantigens bypass normal antigen presentation by binding large quantities of lymphocytes directly to MHC class II receptors on APCs, activating up to 20% of total T cells, causing massive cytokine burst leading to overwhelming inflammatory response, shock, endothelial leakage, multiorgan failure, death.

Enterobacter cloacae intermediate to ertapenem, but susceptible to meropenem and cefepime

cohort_answer.text: Serratia: Carbapenemase (enzyme inactivation) by SME (oxa-48 also can show this pattern). Pseudomonas: RND efflux pump MexAB-OprM (meropenem/doripenem, but not imipenem, are substrates of this efflux system). S. aureus/dapto: Target-site alteration (change in bacterial cell membrane composition) - dapto requires calcium to become positively charged and interacts with negatively charged lipid moieties on membrane to kill; increased positive charge on membrane prevents dapto action. E. gallinarum: Target-site alteration - VanC (specific to E. gallinarum); vancomycin binds terminal D-ala-D-ala residues of growing PG cell wall; VanA isolates show high MICs to Vancomycin and Teicoplanin, VanB/VanC often have lower MICs to Vancomycin and are S to Teicoplanin. Enterobacter cloacae: Hyperexpression of ampC + porin change combination.

parts.text: What is a treatment for MRSA prosthetic valve endocarditis according to IDSA guidelines (drug, route, dose, duration)?

cohort_answer.text: Vancomycin IV (~30 mg/kg/d in 2 doses, target trough 10-20), minimum six weeks. Rifampin IV/PO 900 mg in 3 divided doses, minimum 6 weeks. Gentamicin IV/IM 3 mg/kg/d in 2-3 divided doses, 2 weeks. Gentamicin should be administered for the initial 2 weeks of therapy with either beta-lactam or vancomycin-containing regimens; if a strain is resistant to gentamicin, a fluoroquinolone may be used if the strain is susceptible.

questions.question: AM 23. Kid presents at 2 weeks with bullous impetigo growing S aureus - treated with no issues. Any underlying tests for immunodeficiency? (1) Kid 2 years old presents with 3rd episode of perianal abscess S aureus - any tests for immunodeficiency? (1)

parts.text: What tests for immunodeficiency in each scenario?

cohort_answer.text: Chronic granulomatous disease (CGD, older kid) - diagnosed via neutrophil function testing (nitroblue tetrazolium reduction or dihydrorhodamine 123 flow cytometry). Jobs syndrome/hyper-IgE syndrome (neonate) - total IgE concentration. Other associated: HIV, severe atopic dermatitis, cystic fibrosis. Leukocyte adhesion defect (LAD, neonate) - defective chemotaxis, delayed umbilical cord separation, neutrophilia, predisposition to staph infections. CGD caused by defects in phagocyte oxidase; infections with catalase-positive organisms (Staph aureus, Aspergillus, Burkholderia cepacia complex, Serratia marcescens, Nocardia; outside N. America also Salmonella, Neisseria, Acinetobacter); prophylaxis with Septra + Itraconazole (or Vori/Posa).

questions.question: Purulent cellulitis in homeless individual.

parts.text: Name the two most likely pathogens to cause this
Tells you he cut it in sea water concerning for vibrio vulnificus, what empiric oral agent could cover all 3 organisms?
He gets allergy to that agent, design two regimens with a single daily IV and/or BID oral that could be used instead of above.
Name 5 organisms (genus and species) of acute water SSTI.

questions.model_answer:
a) The two most likely pathogens causing purulent cellulitis in this population: Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA) and Streptococcus pyogenes (group A Streptococcus).
b) Doxycycline is a reasonable single empiric oral agent providing activity against MRSA, streptococci, and Vibrio vulnificus.
c) Two alternative regimens (single daily-dose IV and/or twice-daily oral, maximum two drugs each): Regimen 1 - ceftriaxone 1-2 g IV once daily (covers Streptococcus and Vibrio) plus trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole PO twice daily (covers MRSA). Regimen 2 - ertapenem 1 g IV once daily (covers Streptococcus, Vibrio, and other gram-negatives) plus linezolid PO/IV 600 mg twice daily (covers MRSA and Streptococcus).
d) Five organisms causing acute water-associated skin/soft tissue infection: Vibrio vulnificus, Aeromonas hydrophila, Mycobacterium marinum, Erysipelothrix rhusiopathiae, and Edwardsiella tarda.
questions.beyond_mandell: Specific antibiotic dosing regimens reflect standard clinical practice/IDSA SSTI guideline principles beyond the exact Mandell text.

questions.question: You see a 9 month-old child presenting with fever, irritability, and hypotension. They have a diffuse erythematous rash involving the face, trunk, and extremities, with regions of desquamation and bull formation. The lips are cracked but there is no oral involvement. Application of pressure adjacent to a bulla leads to it rupturing.

parts.text: What is the name of the most likely condition?
What is the toxin responsible for this condition?
MIS-C is also on the differentiation diagnosis. Name TWO organ systems and ONE finding in each system that are on the WHO diagnostic criteria.

questions.model_answer:
a) Most likely condition: Staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome (TSS).
b) Toxin responsible: toxic shock syndrome toxin-1 (TSST-1) (a superantigen).
c) MIS-C WHO diagnostic criteria - 2 organ systems and 1 finding in each: (1) Cardiovascular - hypotension or shock (or evidence of myocardial dysfunction, e.g., elevated troponin/BNP, pericarditis, valvulitis, or coronary abnormalities); (2) Gastrointestinal - abdominal pain, vomiting, or diarrhea.
questions.beyond_mandell: WHO/CDC MIS-C case definition criteria are not covered in this Mandell Staph aureus chapter.

questions.question: Based on the best available evidence, what is the shortest available duration of therapy for the following conditions, assuming clinical improvement and defervesced at 48 hours in each case on therapy?

parts.text: Uncomplicated, fully-susceptible E coli pyelonephritis without any stones or obstruction?
Klebsiella bacteremia due to a now-passed stone with no evidence of abscess or complication?
Fully-susceptible, pulmonary TB without dissemination?
Hospital-acquired S. aureus bacteremia with line removal, repeat blood cultures at 48 hours negative, TEE negative for IE, and no other signs of metastatic infection?
Community acquired pneumonia without microbiologic diagnosis not on oxygen?
Perforated diverticulitis status post OR for washout without any concern of residual abscess per the surgeon?

questions.model_answer: Shortest evidence-based durations: Uncomplicated, fully-susceptible E. coli pyelonephritis (no stones/obstruction) - 5 days (e.g., with a fluoroquinolone); 7 days if using a beta-lactam or TMP-SMX. Klebsiella bacteremia from a passed stone, no abscess/complication - 7 days. Fully-susceptible pulmonary TB without dissemination - 6 months (2 months RIPE + 4 months INH/RIF), the shortest standard regimen. Hospital-acquired S. aureus bacteremia with line removed, negative repeat cultures at 48h, negative TEE, no metastatic infection - 14 days (uncomplicated bacteremia). Community-acquired pneumonia without microbiologic diagnosis, not on oxygen, afebrile by 48h - 5 days (minimum per IDSA/ATS 2019 CAP guideline). Perforated diverticulitis status post operative washout with adequate source control, no residual abscess - 4 days (per fixed-duration antibiotic data, e.g., STOP-IT trial approach).
questions.beyond_mandell: IDSA/ATS CAP guideline (2019), STOP-IT trial (complicated intra-abdominal infection duration), and short-course gram-negative bacteremia trial data (e.g., Yahav et al. 2019) - not covered in this Mandell Staph aureus chapter.

questions.question: Please complete the following table regarding mechanisms of resistance

parts.text: Complete the table (Organism / Antibiotic / Mechanism / Gene associated) for: Enterobacter cloacae (Ceftazidime), MRSA (Daptomycin), Neisseria gonorrhea (Ceftriaxone)

questions.model_answer:
Enterobacter cloacae / Ceftazidime: Mechanism - derepressed hyperproduction of chromosomal AmpC cephalosporinase; Gene - ampC (chromosomal, with regulatory ampR/ampD mutations).
MRSA / Daptomycin: Mechanism - cell membrane remodeling that increases positive surface charge and repels the cationic lipopeptide, plus membrane thickening reducing drug penetration; Gene - mprF (and yycFG/walKR system mutations).
Neisseria gonorrhoeae / Ceftriaxone: Mechanism - altered penicillin-binding protein 2 with reduced cephalosporin affinity, compounded by efflux pump overexpression and porin loss; Gene - penA (mosaic PBP2), with contributions from mtrR and penB.
questions.beyond_mandell: Resistance mechanism/gene detail is general clinical microbiology knowledge, not specific to this Mandell chapter.

questions.question: Group of patients develop nausea/vomiting/diaphoresis approximately 3 hrs (range 1-7) after eating ham.

parts.text: What are the most likely organisms and syndrome?
How do you test for it?

cohort_answer.text: S. aureus (SEA-SEV toxins) or B. cereus - preformed enterotoxin-mediated; short incubation 1-8h, illness generally self-limiting <24h. Testing: Clinical diagnosis; can do stool cultures to rule out other causes; blood cultures if unstable.

questions.question: Q37 (2014). Antibacterial Mechanism of Resistance. What is the mechanism of resistance in the following scenarios: Serratia (Ertapenem R, Imipenem R, Meropenem R, CFTx S); Pseudomonas (Meropenem R, Imipenem S); E. gallinarum (Vancomycin R); E. cloacae (Cefepime S, Meropenem S, Ceftazidime R, Ertapenem R); MRSA (Daptomycin R); MRSA (Linezolid R)

parts.text: State the mechanism of resistance for each scenario

cohort_answer.text: Serratia: Serratia marcescens enzyme (SME) - carbapenemase Class A. Pseudomonas: MexAB-OprM efflux cassette. E. gallinarum: VanC gene presence (chromosomal). E. cloacae: intrinsic resistance to inducible AmpC (R to beta-lactams); OXA-48 (R to Erta, S to Mero with additional efflux pump or porin). MRSA Daptomycin R: mprF gene (phosphatidylglycerol lysyltransferase). MRSA Linezolid R: 23S RNA G2576T point mutation.

questions.question: Q59 (2003 AM). Antibacterial Mechanism of Resistance

parts.text: a) What is the % resistance to clindamycin in S. aureus?
b) What is the mechanism of clindamycin resistance?

cohort_answer.text: a) ~5% for MSSA, 25% for MRSA. b) Alteration in 23S rRNA of 50S ribosomal subunit via methylation of adenine (modified binding site for ribosome inhibitors), usually plasmid mediated ('MLS type of resistance', seen in S. aureus, S. pyogenes, B. fragilis; encoded by ermA or ermC genes in S. aureus, can be inducible or constitutive). Also: mutations in ribosomal RNA/50S ribosomal proteins; inactivation of drug by plasmid-mediated 3-lincomycin 4-clindamycin O-nucleotidyltransferase in some staph/bacteroides species. Enterobacteriaceae, Pseudomonas spp., Acinetobacter spp. intrinsically resistant due to poor outer membrane permeability.

Q10 (2016 PM)
When to use cefoxitin disc for isolates of S. aureus and CNST

parts.text: This predicts resistance to which abx?

cohort_answer.text: Oxacillin disk diffusion testing is not reliable for detecting oxacillin resistance and cefoxitin should be used as surrogate instead, because cefoxitin is a better inducer of mecA gene and thus more reliable than oxacillin (detection of BORSA)

parts.text: A) Most likely cause of neutropenia, other options for treatment?
B) List 3 approved in Canada

cohort_answer.text:
Vancomycin induced neutropenia (occurs mostly after minimum 7 days on therapy, majority at least 20 days after starting). Other options: treat febrile neutropenia, likely needs combo of PipTazo + Linezolid

questions.question: Woman with AVR (aortic valve replacement); 3 weeks later, sternal wound red, infected and patient febrile. Surgeon opens it up, debrides, packs wound. Cultures from wound and blood + S. aureus. Pt on Cloxacillin. Pt still febrile, wound still looks bad.

parts.text: List 2 sources for her ongoing fever
What tests would your order?
How would you treat this patient (give abx, mode of admin, frequency and duration)

cohort_answer.text: Sources of fever: MRSA (resistant to clox), mediastinitis/mediastinal abscess persisting, prosthetic valve IE. Tests: susceptibility testing on S. aureus isolate, CT chest to rule out mediastinitis/abscess, TEE. Treatment: Vancomycin based on weight and Cr until susceptibilities available; for mediastinitis, surgical debridement plus antibiotics (vancomycin if MRSA, cloxacillin if MSSA, increase frequency to q4h/consider continuous infusion); duration 2-3 weeks after sternal resection and pectoral flap, or 4-6 weeks if residual rib/sternal bone infection risk

questions.question: 8 month old child with fever, tachycardia, tachypnea, hypertension, irritability. Has cracked lips, no other oral involvement. No conjunctivitis. Confluent erythematous rash over face, trunk, and diaper region. Positive Nikolsky sign.

parts.text: Most likely diagnosis (0.5)
What toxin is responsible for this (0.5)
